newsitem.title: YEMEN: High voter turnout delays Yemen poll results.
newsitem.headline: High voter turnout delays Yemen poll results.

text.p: Yemen said on Monday it was delaying the announcement of initial results in its first parliamentary elections since a 1994 civil war because high voter turnout had slowed counting.

"We are keen for accurate figures...The (first) results will be announced by tomorrow (Tuesday) noon (0900 GMT)," Saeed al-Hekaimi, spokesman for the Supreme Election Committee, told a news conference.
Yemeni officials had earlier said they expected initial results by Monday afternoon.
Hekaimi attributed high turnout to new voting cards that carried election symbols for many candidates in Sunday's ballot, overshadowed by two fatal shootings in which nine people died.
This encouraged many of Yemen's illiterate voters to take part, swelling turnout -- officially put at 80 percent although international monitors believed it was closer to 60 percent.
Witnesses said the capital Sanaa appeared calm on Monday as military police armed with AK-47 assault rifles manned polling stations while votes were counted.

Hekaimi said voting would be repeated in a constituency in Dhamar, 100 km (60 miles) south of Sanaa -- scene of some election violence -- after voters refused to cast ballots because the symbol of their candidate was missing due to an administrative error. He gave no new date.
Hekaimi also reported "a new incident of election violence in Dhamar" but declined to elaborate.

An election observer told Reuters that three people were wounded, two seriously, after supporters of the Dhamar candidate whose symbol was missing opened fire on a car carrying backers of his rival. Both candidates are local sheikhs.

Before voting began, a soldier started shooting at people randomly at a polling station in the town of Mukayras, killing five soldiers and three civilians, Interior Minister Hussein Mohammad Arab said.

Arab said security officials were investigating the incident but no political motive had been established. "We were expecting more incidents because some are discontented with holding general elections in Yemen," he said. He did not elaborate.
He said one of the victims of the first attack was a member of Yemen's ruling party, the General People's Congress (GPC).
Also on Sunday, a man refused access to a polling station in Dhamar fired on a security officer who died after the attack, an election observer said.

The incidents raised to four the number of election-related fatal attacks. A man was killed when clashes broke out between supporters of the GPC and its junior coalition partner, the Islamist Islah Party, in Ibb on April 20 and a child was killed in Taiz on Thursday when gunmen opened fire on a GPC rally.
Election observers said the violence was not surprising as many Yemenis routinely carry Kalashnikov assault rifles and other firearms. Some incidents are related to tribal strife.
One election observer said the voting and counting seemed free of violations in several polling stations visited.
Western diplomats expect President Ali Abdullah Saleh's GPC and Islah to retain power.

The main opposition Yemen Socialist Party, some of whose former leaders launched the separatist campaign that sparked civil war, and three others boycotted the polls due to alleged irregularities. The government denied the charges.
A total of 2,306 candidates, including 17 women, stood for the 301 parliamentary seats, either under the banner of 12 parties or as independents.
